newsitem.title: USA: US Jan housing starts bounce evokes scant reaction.
newsitem.headline: US Jan housing starts bounce evokes scant reaction.

text.p: U.S. housing starts bounced back, though less strongly than expected, in January, eliciting little market reaction and having no particular implications for Federal Reserve monetary policy.
Housing starts rose 2.0 percent to an annualized rate of 1.350 million in January from a revised annualized rate of 1.323 million in December.
While economists had anticipated a bounce, a Reuters poll had forecast a somewhat stronger head of steam, eliciting an average forecast of 1.42 million starts for January.

The housing data were released at the same time as weekly jobless claims figures. If anything, the latter evoked an even stronger picture of the labor market than economists had forecast. Any gains the market might have scored on friendly housing data were thus offset by the less-than-friendly news contained in the jobless claims figures.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year Treasury bond, which was down about a quarter of a point before the data came out, weakened mildly just after the reports before returning to earlier levels.
"Housing is clearly weakening from the peaks we were seeing last spring and summer. That's nothing new," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
But Feinman said the headlines of the last couple of months might present a more exaggerated picture of housing market weakness than is actually the case.
"First, bad weather has taken a toll on housing activity in the Midwest," he said. "And second, most of the declines of the last two months have occurred in the multi-family sector.
"Bigger ticket, single-family construction hasn't weakened in the last two months, though it is below the peaks of spring and summer," said Feinman.
Permits for new housing construction declined 1.9 percent in January but remained above their fourth-quarter average, Feinman said, predicting that housing construction would rebound in the spring.

"Consumer fundamentals are in great shape, the labor market is strong, confidence is high, and while mortgage rates have moved up from a year ago, they are still at pretty reasonable levels," said Feinman.

"You have to look at permits (to start new construction) as well as actual starts and permits are holding up at a reasonably high level," said Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp Global Finance.

The locus of strength in housing also shifted in January, Bhagavatula said. The government said starts jumped 22.2 percent in the Northeast and 29.8 percent in the West. Starts fell 13.2 percent in the Midwest and 6.8 percent in the South.
"That is consistent with broader economic activity," said Bhagavatula. "California has been coming back and the Northeast is doing a little better."
Feinman said the January housing data underscored that while the housing sector will not be a major source of impetus to the overall economy, neither will it be a drag.
Bhagavatula also said the housing sector is now a neutral sector for the economy.
But he said it could be a drag by the end of the year.
"The assumption is that pent-up demand for housing will be pretty much satisfied by then," he said.
